column3: It closely repeats Moses seeking refuge in his and their shared Lord against an immediate violent assault, directly clarifying the focus's threatened stance.
Elijah's call to fear God offers a broad counterpoint to the focus's arrogant unbeliever, but adds no refuge or Pharaoh setting.
Noah's refuge in his Lord from an ignorant request shows protective recourse to God, though the danger is self-incurred rather than political violence.
Moses entrusts guidance and the final outcome to his Lord, reinforcing his refusal to yield the dispute with Pharaoh to Pharaoh's authority.
Pharaoh's stated intent to kill Moses is the immediate threat answered by the focus's declaration of refuge.
The prayer for protection from harmful presence supplies a concise parallel of seeking refuge in the Lord, though without the tyrant or accounting horizon.
Moses addresses Pharaoh as a messenger from the Lord of all worlds, establishing the authority behind the focus's appeal before their confrontation.
Its denial of any protector on the turning Day directly joins the focus's refuge language to the arrogant person's disbelief in accountability.
Pharaoh's question about the Lord of Moses and Aaron frames the contested authority, but it is less specific than the shared Lordship already established.
Affirming the Day of Recompense is the direct positive opposite of the focus's defining disbelief in the Day of Account.
Measured redress after aggression concerns just response to injury, a distant resonance with threatened protection rather than Moses's refuge.
Human ingratitude toward his Lord provides a moral counterpart to the focus's arrogant rejection, though it lacks threat and the Day of Account.
Moses seeks refuge from being among the ignorant when challenged by his people; the formula parallels but the situation does not add to Pharaoh's threat.
The regime's prior command to kill the believers' sons supplies the coercive pattern that makes Moses's refuge in the next verses necessary.
The unchangeable words of the Lord and absence of refuge besides Him give a general theological support, but no immediate threatened-speaker scene.
Denial of the Day of Recompense repeats the focus's criterion for the arrogant adversary, though it adds no protective response.
The warning that no one can save Pharaoh's people from God's might joins present royal power to the very accountability Pharaoh's posture denies.
A calculated gift from the Lord invokes recompense, but its reward scene adds little to the focus's account-denying persecutor.
The command to seek refuge in the Lord of humanity strongly parallels the focus's appeal to shared divine lordship for protection.
The legitimacy of defending oneself after wrong offers only a broad counterpart to protection from aggression.
Iblis's rebellion against his Lord and his hostile progeny illuminate arrogant opposition in general, but not Moses's threatened refuge.
Failure to believe in God the Great is related to the focus's unbelieving oppressor, yet it omits the Day of Account and the conflict.
The believing man explicitly contests killing Moses for saying his Lord is God, directly continuing the danger and shared authority underlying the focus.
Glorifying the name of the great Lord supplies a broad reverent contrast to arrogance but adds no further context.
Confessing denial of the Day of Recompense directly identifies the moral stance attributed to the arrogant one in the focus.
Past powerful peoples had no protector from God when seized for sins, clarifying why refuge is sought from a mortal tyrant and why arrogance fails.
The magicians name the Lord of Moses and Aaron, publicly displacing Pharaoh's claimed authority, though this repeats the confrontation's basic frame.
Trust in God as my Lord and your Lord, who holds every creature, is a close counterpart to the focus's shared-Lord refuge against hostile power.
The promised event exposes who has weaker support, broadly limiting persecutors' power but not specifically addressing refuge or accounting.
The Lord's sovereignty over heavens, earth, and horizons magnifies the authority invoked in the focus, without adding to its threat.
The confession that God is my Lord without associating partners contrasts directly with Pharaoh-like self-exaltation, though outside the persecution scene.
Resisting aggression provides a broad response to oppression, but does not explain refuge in the Lord.
The Mighty Forgiver as Lord of all realms combines authority and mercy, a useful theological frame for Moses's appeal but not a close narrative parallel.
A plea for forgiveness on the Day the account is established connects Lordship and accountability, complementing the focus's account-denying adversary.
Lot's wish for strength or a formidable support echoes a threatened prophet's need for protection, but contrasts with Moses's actual recourse to God.
Seeking refuge in God before recitation gives a general protective practice, now less informative after the closer refuge parallels.
The oath by the Day of Resurrection supplies only a general eschatological horizon for the Day of Account.
The failed appeal to a mountain for protection shows that no created refuge can resist God's command, qualifying the focus's true refuge.
People in the Fire ask for increased punishment for those who led them there, offering only a distant consequence for arrogant misguidance.
God's preservation and the test of belief in the hereafter provide broad themes of protection and accountability, without a direct inter-ayah scene.
Proportionate retaliation and forgiveness concern ethical redress, only indirectly related to the focus's threatened protection.
The magicians' identification of the Lord of Moses and Aaron reinforces the rejection of Pharaoh's authority, but repeats the earlier formula.
Seeking refuge in the Lord of daybreak closely parallels the focus's protective appeal, adding the image of escape from emerging harm.
Wrongdoers who transgress face painful punishment, giving a consequence frame for the arrogant aggressor in the focus.
Fear of standing before one's Lord is the positive counterpart to denial of account, but it adds little after more direct Day-of-Recompense cards.
Jesus's declaration that God is my Lord and your Lord strongly echoes shared lordship and warns of grave consequences, though in another polemical setting.
The command to endure and the good outcome for the God-fearing offers a broad prophetic counterpart to Moses's threatened situation.
The magicians' declaration of return to their Lord gives a fearless response to Pharaoh's coercion, though it no longer adds the refuge formula.
God is our Lord and your Lord, with eventual gathering to Him, closely echoes shared lordship and accountability but lacks an immediate threat.
Racing toward forgiveness and Paradise gives a positive eschatological alternative to account-denying arrogance, but is otherwise distant.
Being veiled from their Lord on that Day gives a specific consequence for those who reject accountability, though it does not advance the protection theme.
Each soul is repaid for what it earned without injustice and God is swift in account, directly defining the Day denied by the focus's adversary.
Return to the Lord affirms ultimate accountability, but adds little beyond the more explicit accounting verses.
God repays every soul for what it earned and is swift in account, directly supports the focus's Day-of-Account criterion.
Abraham's immediate submission to the Lord of worlds is a broad antithesis to arrogant refusal, with little further connection.
The false protector abandons his allies when punishment approaches, contrasting with Moses's dependable refuge in God but in a different setting.
Magnifying the Lord provides a compact reversal of the arrogant self-magnification that motivates the threat in the focus.
Jesus calls people to worship my Lord and your Lord, a close shared-Lord formula, but it does not involve refuge from violence.
Return to the Lord after worldly punishment gestures toward final judgment, but adds little to Moses's threatened present scene.
The sovereign who gives life and death is to be believed and followed, providing a broad alternative to Pharaoh's authority and unbelief.
Mary's appeal for refuge in the Merciful from a perceived threat closely parallels protective recourse, though not its shared-Lord formulation.
Believers receive their reward with their Lord, who is swift in account, but the general reward statement adds little to prior account verses.
God is our Lord and your Lord and each bears its own deeds, closely joins shared lordship with individual accountability.
God seals every arrogant tyrant's heart, directly naming the character type from which Moses seeks refuge in the focus.
The magicians' faith in the Lord of all worlds is a public reversal of Pharaoh's authority, though redundant with their fuller naming earlier.
True believers prostrate and praise their Lord without arrogance, forming the direct moral opposite of the focus's arrogant unbeliever.
Seeking protection from created beings increases oppression, sharply contrasting the focus's refuge in the true Lord rather than a false protector.
A ruined garden leads to regret over associating partners with the Lord, a distant aftermath of pride rather than a refuge scene.
Pharaoh asks what the Lord of all worlds is, directly framing his challenge to the authority Moses invokes for protection.
God's unanswerable judgment and swift account support ultimate authority, but add little after explicit account and shared-Lord texts.
The dying person's request for delay exposes a belated appeal to the Lord, a distant contrast to Moses's timely refuge.
It names the pride of those disputing God's signs and commands seeking refuge in God, an exceptionally close later-surah restatement of the focus.
Patience for the Lord gives a general prophetic posture under pressure, without adding to refuge or the account-denier.
The pattern of receiving messengers with what people dislike and then killing some thematically parallels Pharaoh's killing threat against Moses.
The command to seek refuge in the Lord from satanic promptings is a close protective formula, though the enemy differs from the focus's human tyrant.
Moses states that God's praise and self-sufficiency are unaffected by universal disbelief, a broad answer to the focus's unbeliever.
Worship of the Lord of this House is a general alternative to misplaced allegiance, adding little to the immediate conflict.
Moses rebukes those who call truth magic, continuing the prophetic contest with Pharaoh-like denial though without protection language.
A messenger's reward being with the Lord of worlds affirms divine service, but does not clarify Moses's threatened refuge.
Moses warns against fabricating lies about God lest punishment destroy them, giving a related confrontation with Pharaoh's magicians.
The Lord's action against Aad gives a broad precedent for judgment on powerful arrogance, without the focus's specific relations.
Moses's sea miracle displays divine rescue from Pharaoh, a meaningful narrative outcome but only indirectly clarifies this declaration of refuge.
The Lord of the heavens and great throne expresses supreme sovereignty, but is redundant after closer shared-Lord and Pharaoh cards.
The magicians' faith in the Lord of all worlds repeats their submission without adding to the focus beyond earlier parallel entries.
The repeated statement that a messenger asks no reward from the Lord of worlds does not clarify refuge, arrogance, or the Day of Account.
Mocking demand for one's portion before the Day of Account adds a related but limited instance of resisting future reckoning.
The same no-reward formula remains unrelated to the focus after its prior occurrence.
The promised rewards for the Day of Account retain only the accounting term, without threat or refuge.
The third no-reward repetition adds no marginal understanding of the focus.
The division between believers and nonbelievers, with the Lord knowing corrupters, gives a general contrast to the focus's unbelieving arrogant one.
Pharaoh and his leaders call toward the Fire and receive no help on Resurrection Day, directly supplies the tyrant's ultimate consequence.
The driving toward the Lord on that Day supplies an accountability horizon, but does not add beyond earlier judgment texts.
The prophetic covenant to believe and support a confirming messenger offers only a broad contrast to rejecting Moses.
The Most Generous Lord gives a general attribute of the authority Moses invokes, but no threat or refuge relation.
People in punishment blame those who brought it on them, a distant consequence of misleading arrogance.
Reverent fear of the Lord contrasts with the focus's arrogant unbelief, but is now a general repetition.
The shade of black smoke does not clarify the focus's refuge, adversary, or Day of Account.
Human willing is subject to God, Lord of worlds, broadly limits the tyrant's autonomy but adds little beyond stronger sovereignty passages.
The search for a nursing household for infant Moses is unrelated to the focus's threatened prophetic appeal.
Praise to God, Lord of worlds, closes with the authority Moses invokes but adds no specific protection or accountability detail.
The wife of Pharaoh asks her Lord to save her from Pharaoh and his deeds and from the wrongdoers, an exceptionally close counterpart to Moses's refuge from the tyrant.
Moses leaves the city fearful and asks his Lord to save him from the wrongdoing people, directly pairing danger from Pharaoh's regime with divine deliverance.
Moses tells his Lord that he fears they will kill him, supplying an explicit earlier formulation of the lethal danger answered by the focus's refuge.
Moses acknowledges a charge against him and fears that Pharaoh's people will kill him, directly clarifying the mortal threat in the focus.
Moses directs his people to seek help in God and remain steadfast under Pharaoh, a close communal counterpart to his personal refuge in the focus.
Moses's people pray for deliverance by God's mercy from the disbelieving people, closely matching protective appeal against an unbelieving oppressor.
God protects the believing man of Pharaoh's family from the evils they plotted, supplying the immediate surah outcome of reliance against the regime.
The arrogant enter the gates of Hell, directly providing the final consequence for the arrogant person from whom Moses seeks refuge.
Pharaoh threatens the magicians with mutilation and death, showing the coercive violence of the ruler opposed to Moses.
Moses says he fled from Pharaoh's people when he feared them, a narrative counterpart to later seeking the Lord's protection.
Moses's people declare reliance on God and ask not to be made a trial for the wrongdoing people, reinforcing faithful dependence under oppression.
When incited by hostile prompting, the command is to seek refuge in God, a general but exact protective response parallel.
The command to seek refuge in God from harmful prompting supplies another explicit refuge formula, though not the Pharaoh setting.
God's sufficiency for His servant frames the confidence implicit in Moses's refusal to let Pharaoh determine his safety.
Believers answer a threat by declaring God sufficient and the best guardian, a close response pattern to Moses's danger.
The oppressed ask their Lord for a protector and helper against a wrongful town, a worldly counterpart to refuge from coercive power.
Doubting the Hour when God's promise is announced provides a related form of the focus's denial of the Day of Account.
Joseph asks his Lord to turn away a coercive plot, a broader prophetic instance of seeking divine protection from human pressure.
